372.title: Only a messenger
372.hook: Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers passed before him (3:144)
372.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet as the final messenger while holding that he was a mortal man; 3:144 and Abu Bakr's words at his death are often recalled when teaching that faith rests on God, not on any person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, after Uhud: faint not nor grieve. Your line was days turn. Did you take one step after a setback? Day three hundred seventy-two.

In the chaos at Uhud, someone shouted that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had been killed. He hadn't; he was wounded and hidden by his companions. But the rumor ran through the army faster than the truth. Some men put down their swords and sat. Some started thinking about running. If he was gone, what was left? The commentators say a verse came down about that moment. And years later, on the day he really did die, someone stood up and read that verse aloud.
screen: `A RUMOR AT UHUD.` → `IF HE WAS GONE, WHAT WAS LEFT?` → `READ ALOUD YEARS LATER.`

segments.voice: The verse is 3:144. In Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him." Then it asks: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back doesn't harm God at all. It's a startling verse to find in scripture: a plain statement that the Prophet is mortal, and that faith isn't meant to hang on one human life. Now, the second scene. Medina, in the year 632. The Prophet has died in the room of his wife A'ishah. Umar, one of the strongest of the companions, can't accept it. He stands in the mosque insisting it isn't true. Then Abu Bakr arrives, the Prophet's oldest friend. He goes in, uncovers the Prophet's face, and kisses him. Then he comes out to the crowd. According to the account in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; and whoever worships God, God is alive and does not die. And he recites 3:144. The report says it was as if people had never heard the verse before, and then everyone was reciting it. Umar said his legs gave way when he heard it. The message outlives the messenger. Muslims love the Prophet deeply; many say they love him more than their own families. And still the Qur'an itself says he was a man, a messenger, one in a long line. What he brought, the prayer, the Qur'an, the way of living, is meant to keep going after him.
screen: `A RUMOR IN THE BATTLE` · `MUHAMMAD IS BUT A MESSENGER` · `ABU BAKR AT THE DOOR` · `GOD IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE` · then, large: `THE MESSAGE OUTLIVES THE MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of someone who taught you something that mattered and who is no longer in your life: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away, someone who died. Don't dwell on the loss. Ask instead: what of theirs is still alive in me? A habit, a phrase, a way of treating people. Name it. Feel how it outlasted them. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them. The bell holds the time.
Only a messenger. Muhammad is but a messenger, like those before him, from 3:144: the verse Abu Bakr recited on the day the Prophet died. Today's word.
Your line: the message outlives the messenger. Today, do the thing that person taught you, once, on purpose, so it keeps going. Day three hundred seventy-two.

options: agree with Umar to calm people.

what it means: the Qur'an says plainly he is a mortal messenger, and faith is meant to outlive him.
what a scholar hears: a verse revealed for a false rumor at Uhud, then recited by Abu Bakr at the real death in 632, as Bukhari reports.

373.title: Had you been harsh
373.hook: by Allah's mercy he was gentle; had he been harsh they'd have left, so consult them (3:159)
373.howItsDone: Muslims treat shura, consultation, as a principle for families, mosques and communities; mosque committees, family decisions and Islamic political thought all draw on 3:159 and 42:38, with differing views on how binding consultation is.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Muhammad is but a messenger, and Abu Bakr's words on the day he died. Your line was the message outlives the messenger. Did you pass on something you were taught? Day three hundred seventy-three.

Before Uhud, the Prophet ﷺ held a meeting. Should they stay inside Medina and defend the streets, or march out to meet the army in the open? He leaned toward staying. Many of the younger men, eager to fight, wanted to go out. He listened, and he went out with them. And we know how it ended. So imagine the advice you'd expect next: stop asking them. You know better. The Qur'an says the opposite.
screen: `A MEETING BEFORE UHUD.` → `HE LISTENED, AND WENT OUT.` → `THE EXPECTED ADVICE: STOP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:159 in Pickthall's words: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." Then: so pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult with them in the affair. And when you've decided, put your trust in God. Look at the order. First, gentleness is called a mercy from God, not a weakness. Second, the people around the Prophet would have scattered if he'd been harsh. The verse says so, plainly, about the best of leaders. Third, right after a decision made by consultation went badly, the command is: keep consulting. The word is shawirhum, consult them, from the same root as shura, consultation. A whole surah, the forty-second, is called ash-Shura, and in 42:38 it describes believers as people whose affairs are settled by counsel among themselves. Scholars have long debated how binding consultation is on a leader, and what form it should take, from a ruler's council to a family deciding where to live. But the core is simple. Ask the people affected. Listen. Then decide, and trust God with the outcome, without second-guessing forever. And there's a detail worth noticing. The Prophet, Muslims believe, received revelation. If anyone could have skipped the meeting, it was him. The hadith collections are full of him asking his companions, his wives, even the young, what they thought.
screen: `GENTLENESS IS A MERCY` · `HARSHNESS SCATTERS PEOPLE` · `SHAWIRHUM: CONSULT THEM, STILL` · `DECIDE, THEN TRUST GOD` · then, large: `HAD YOU BEEN HARSH, THEY WOULD HAVE LEFT.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of a decision in front of you that touches someone else: a plan at home, something at work, a change in the family. Picture the person it affects most. Ask yourself honestly: have I asked them? Then imagine the conversation, and imagine yourself listening, gently, not waiting for your turn to speak. Decide who you'll ask today, and what you'll ask. The bell holds the time.
Shura. Consultation, deciding together by counsel. From 3:159, consult them in the affair, and from the surah named after it. Today's word.
Your line: gentle, and consult. Today, before you decide something that touches someone else, ask their opinion, and listen to the whole answer. Day three hundred seventy-three.

what it means: gentleness is a mercy, harshness drives people away, and the people affected should be consulted.
what a scholar hears: the command came after Uhud, where consultation had gone badly; and a long debate over whether shura binds the leader or only informs him.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the council before Uhud)

374.title: Every soul tastes death
374.hook: every soul shall taste death, and the world is the enjoyment of delusion (3:185)
374.howItsDone: Muslims recite 'every soul will taste death' at funerals, in condolences and in sermons, and it is often carved on gravestones; remembering death is encouraged as a way to live with purpose, not in fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shura: consultation, and a gentleness the Qur'an calls a mercy. Your line was gentle, and consult. Did you ask someone before deciding? Day three hundred seventy-four.

Walk through an old Muslim cemetery in Istanbul, Cairo or Lahore and you'll often see the same Arabic words carved on stone after stone, sometimes above the gate. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. Every soul will taste death. It isn't hidden in a back room of the faith. It's at the entrance. And it isn't only for funerals; it's said in ordinary sermons and quoted in condolence messages. Today, the verse on those stones.
screen: `CARVED ON THE STONES.` → `ABOVE THE GATE.` → `NOT HIDDEN. AT THE ENTRANCE.`

segments.voice: Al 'Imran 185, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Every soul will taste of death." The same sentence appears in two other surahs as well, 21:35 and 29:57, so this is a line the Qur'an returns to. Notice the verb. Not every soul will die, but every soul will taste death. Dha'iqa, from dhaqa, to taste. Tasting is something you do once, personally, with your own mouth. Nobody can taste it for you. And a taste passes; it isn't the whole meal. Many commentators read that as a quiet hint: death is something the soul goes through, not where it ends. The verse goes on: you'll be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is drawn away from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won. Then it ends, again in Pickthall's words: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." The Arabic is mata' al-ghurur. Mata' is provision, things you use for a while, like supplies for a trip. Ghurur is deception, the kind that flatters you into forgetting. The world isn't called evil here. It's called useful, and easy to be fooled by. A hadith in Tirmidhi tells people to remember often the destroyer of pleasures, meaning death. Another, in Bukhari, says: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. The point isn't gloom. Travelers enjoy the road. They just don't forget where they're going.
screen: `THE SAME LINE, THREE TIMES` · `TASTE: ONCE, PERSONALLY, AND PASSING` · `MATA': SUPPLIES FOR A TRIP` · `A STRANGER, OR A TRAVELER` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle, and you can stop at any point. If you're grieving right now, just breathe and skip ahead. When the bell starts, sit comfortably, and let yourself think, calmly, that your life has an end you don't know the date of. Not with fear. Like a traveler checking the ticket. Then ask one question: if this were a trip, what supplies am I carrying that I won't need, and what am I forgetting to pack? Let one answer come. The bell holds the time.
Every soul tastes death. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt, from 3:185, and twice more in the Qur'an: a taste, personal, and passing. Today's word.

Your line: every soul tastes it. Today, put down one thing you're carrying that won't matter on the last day, a grudge, a worry about looking good, and pack one thing that will. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: Standing, sitting, lying down
375.hook: those who remember Allah in every posture and reflect on creation: You did not make this in vain (3:190–191)
375.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last verses of Al 'Imran (3:190–200) when they wake for the night prayer, following the Prophet's practice reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, and remember God in whatever posture they're in throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: every soul will taste death, and the world is provision for a journey. Your line was every soul tastes it. Did you set one heavy thing down? Day three hundred seventy-five, and the last day of Al 'Imran.

A boy named Ibn Abbas, the Prophet's young cousin, once spent the night at the house of his aunt Maymunah, one of the Prophet's wives. He lay awake, the way kids do in a house that isn't theirs. Late in the night he saw the Prophet ﷺ get up, sit, look up at the sky, and begin to recite. Bukhari records what he recited: the last verses of Al 'Imran. Today we end the surah with them, under the same sky.
screen: `A BOY AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `THE PROPHET LOOKS AT THE SKY.` → `THE LAST VERSES OF AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Verse 190 says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding. Verse 191 says who they are: those who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth. And what they say, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." Then: glory be to You, protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Three postures. Standing, sitting, lying down. That covers almost every moment of a human life: work, rest, sleep, sickness. The verse is saying remembrance isn't tied to one position or one hour. And the same three postures show up in a hadith about prayer. A sick companion asked how to pray, and the Prophet told him: standing; if you can't, then sitting; if you can't, then on your side. Nobody is too weak to be counted. Then the second act: reflection, tafakkur. Not just looking at the stars, but thinking about them until a conclusion comes out of your mouth: You didn't make this in vain. Batil, the word for in vain, means empty, pointless, false. The night sky says the opposite of pointless. So the surah that began with clear and ambiguous verses ends here. In between: the chosen family, Maryam, a common word, the rope, Uhud and its grief, the message outliving the messenger, gentleness and consultation, death tasted. And at the end, a person under the night sky, in whatever posture they can manage, saying: not in vain.
screen: `SIGNS IN NIGHT AND DAY` · `STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `TAFAKKUR: THINKING IT THROUGH` · `BATIL: EMPTY, POINTLESS` · then, large: `THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.`

segments.voice: Tonight, if the sky is clear, step outside for one minute and look up. For now, when the bell starts, choose your posture: stand, sit, or lie down, whichever your body wants. Picture the night sky: the dark, the scattered lights, the distances. Let the size of it settle on you. Then let one thought form, slowly, the way it did for the people in the verse: this is not pointless. If you pray, you can say the verse's own words: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. The bell holds the time.
Standing. Standing, sitting, and lying down: remembering God in every posture, and reflecting on creation, from 3:191. Today's word.
Your line: not in vain. Tonight, look at the sky before you sleep, and say the line once, standing, sitting, or lying down. Day three hundred seventy-five.

376.title: One soul
376.hook: He created you from a single soul and made its mate, so respect the wombs that bore you (4:1)
376.howItsDone: Muslims hear 4:1 in the khutbat al-hajah, the Prophet's opening sermon recited at many weddings and Friday sermons, and the verse is a basis for keeping ties of kinship, silat al-rahim, a duty stressed throughout Islamic teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Al 'Imran: standing, sitting, lying down, and Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Your line was not in vain. Did you look at the sky? Day three hundred seventy-six, and a new surah.

At a great many Muslim weddings, before the vows, someone stands and gives a short sermon that the Prophet ﷺ used to open important speeches. It quotes three verses. One of them is the first verse of the fourth surah, an-Nisa, the Women. So as two families are being joined, the room hears a verse about where all families came from. Today, that verse, and the opening of a surah that will spend a long time on family, inheritance and fairness.
screen: `A SERMON BEFORE THE VOWS.` → `AN-NISA, THE WOMEN.` → `WHERE ALL FAMILIES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Surah 4 opens by speaking to everyone: O mankind. Then, in Pickthall's words, be careful of your duty to your Lord "Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate." And from those two, the verse says, He spread abroad many men and women. One soul. Nafs wahida. Before any nation, tribe, language or family name, there's a single origin. Every person you'll meet today is, in the verse's picture, a relative. Then comes a phrase that's easy to pass over: be mindful of God, by whom you ask things of one another, and of the arham. Arham means wombs, and by extension it means kinship, the ties of family. And here's the detail. Rahim, womb, comes from the same root as rahma, mercy, and ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes the link explicit: the word for womb is taken from the name ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps its ties, God keeps ties with them. So the surah of the Women begins by placing mothers, wombs and family ties right next to God's own mercy. That's why it fits a wedding. Two families joining are reminded they were already one, and reminded what they owe each other. In the coming days, an-Nisa will get very specific: orphans, inheritance shares, kindness in marriage, neighbors near and far. It all grows out of this first verse. One soul, many people, ties of mercy between them.
screen: `O MANKIND: SPOKEN TO EVERYONE` · `NAFS WAHIDA: ONE SOUL` · `ARHAM: WOMBS, AND KINSHIP` · `RAHIM AND RAHMA: ONE ROOT` · then, large: `FROM A SINGLE SOUL.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of your mother, or whoever carried and raised you. If she's living and you can, plan to call her today. If she has died, or if that relationship is hard, you can simply hold her in mind for a moment, or think of another woman who mothered you. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for her. Then widen the circle: picture the people around you today, strangers included, and remember the verse's claim: from one soul. The bell holds the time.
One soul. Nafs wahida: all people from a single soul and its mate, the opening of an-Nisa, 4:1. Today's word.
Your line: from one soul. Today, call your mother or pray for her, and treat one stranger as the relative the verse says they are. Day three hundred seventy-six.

377.title: The orphans' property
377.hook: give orphans their property and don't swap bad for good (4:2)
377.howItsDone: Muslims treat caring for orphans and guarding their wealth as a serious duty; orphan sponsorship is one of the most common forms of Muslim charity, and Islamic law sets rules for guardians managing a minor's property.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of an-Nisa: all people from one soul, and the ties of the womb. Your line was from one soul. Did you call your mother, or pray for her? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Picture a guardian with a ledger. A child's father has died and left a flock of good sheep, and an uncle is managing them until the child grows up. The uncle has a few sickly sheep of his own. Nobody's checking. He could swap a healthy one for a sick one, once, quietly. Or mix the two flocks together, and let the numbers blur. The second verse of an-Nisa sees that guardian, and that ledger, very clearly.
screen: `A GUARDIAN WITH A LEDGER.` → `A HEALTHY SHEEP FOR A SICK ONE.` → `NOBODY'S CHECKING.`

segments.voice: Surah 4, verse 2, says: give orphans their property. Don't exchange the good for the bad. Don't eat up their wealth by mixing it with your own; that is a great sin. Three precise warnings, aimed at exactly the tricks a guardian might use. Commentators note the setting: Medina after Uhud had many new orphans and widows, and the surah is concerned with them from its first lines. A few verses later, 4:6 gives a whole procedure. Test the orphans as they near the age of marriage. If you find sound judgment in them, rushd, hand their property over. Don't rush to spend it before they grow up. If the guardian is well off, he should take nothing for his work; if he's poor, he may take what is fair. And when you hand it over, call witnesses. Then 4:10 gives a stark picture: those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth are swallowing fire into their bellies. Why so much care? One reason is close to home. The Prophet ﷺ was himself an orphan. His father died before he was born, his mother when he was six. Surah 93 says to him, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?" And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports him holding up two fingers, side by side, and saying that he and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this. The verse turns that warmth into accounting. Love the orphan, yes. And also keep the ledger straight, because theirs is theirs.
screen: `NO SWAPPING, NO MIXING` · `TEST FOR SOUND JUDGMENT, THEN HAND IT OVER` · `THE PROPHET WAS AN ORPHAN` · `TWO FINGERS, SIDE BY SIDE` · then, large: `GIVE ORPHANS THEIR PROPERTY.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of a child somewhere who has lost a parent: someone you know, a family in your community, or the millions you'll never meet. Hold them in mind for a moment without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can ask God to protect them. Then think of one concrete way to help: a sponsorship, a donation to an orphan charity, time with a child who needs an adult. Pick the one you'll actually do. The bell holds the time.
The orphans' property. Theirs to receive in full, with no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses, from 4:2 to 4:10. Today's word.
Your line: theirs is theirs. Today, support an orphan cause in one real way, and return anything you're holding that belongs to someone else. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

378.title: The shares
378.hook: the inheritance verses set shares for daughters, sons, parents, spouses (4:11–12)
378.howItsDone: Muslims divide estates according to the shares in 4:11–12 and 4:176, after debts and any bequest of up to a third; the detailed calculation is a field of Islamic law called 'ilm al-fara'id, and many Muslims write an Islamic will.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orphans' property: no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses. Your line was theirs is theirs. Did you help an orphan cause? Day three hundred seventy-eight, the end of a week.

After Uhud, a widow came to the Prophet ﷺ with her two daughters. Their father, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', had been killed in the battle. And their uncle had taken everything Sa'd owned, the way it was often done in Arabia then: the men who could fight inherited, and women and girls were left out. She asked: who will marry these girls with nothing? The reports say the inheritance verses came down soon after.
screen: `A WIDOW AND TWO DAUGHTERS.` → `THE UNCLE TOOK EVERYTHING.` → `WHO WILL CARE FOR THESE GIRLS?`

segments.voice: The word is mirath, inheritance, from a root meaning to inherit, to be left something. Verses 11 and 12 of an-Nisa set fixed shares, by name. Daughters inherit. Mothers inherit. Wives and husbands inherit from each other. Parents each receive a sixth when there are children. A husband receives half of his wife's estate if she has no children, a quarter if she does; a wife receives a quarter, or an eighth. Sisters and brothers have shares in certain cases. And before anything is divided, the verse says twice, debts are paid and any bequest is honored. In the story, the Prophet sent for the uncle and told him to give the daughters two-thirds, the mother an eighth, and keep the rest. One of the best-known rules is that a son receives twice the share of a daughter. Classical scholars explain it by duties: in Islamic law, a man must pay the bride's dower and support his wife and family, while a woman's wealth is her own, owed to no one. Scholars also point out that in many cases a woman's share equals or exceeds a man's. Muslims today discuss how these rules apply in modern economies, and families and countries handle them in different ways. Another hadith, in Bukhari, adds a limit: a person may leave up to a third by will to people outside the fixed heirs, and the Prophet said even a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than dependent. So the shares turned a family's money from whoever was strongest to a list where everyone has a place. Look back over this week: the message outliving the messenger, consultation, death tasted, the night sky, one soul, the orphans, and now the shares. A surah, and a week, about what we owe each other.
